title: Cellular Processes: Metabolism
summary: This lesson explains how cells obtain and use energy through photosynthesis and cellular respiration. Understanding these processes shows the link between plants and animals in the flow of energy.

sections.heading: What Is Metabolism?
sections.body:
Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions that occur in a cell. It includes two main parts: building up molecules (anabolism) and breaking them down for energy (catabolism). Together, these reactions keep the cell alive and functioning.

Metabolic pathways are series of steps, each catalyzed by a specific enzyme. Enzymes speed up reactions so they can happen at body temperature.

sections.heading: Photosynthesis – Making Food
sections.body:
Photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplasts of plant cells. Light energy is captured by chlorophyll and used to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

The overall equation is: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. The glucose stores chemical energy that can later be released by respiration.

Plants store some glucose as starch and use the rest for growth, repair, and reproduction.

sections.heading: Cellular Respiration – Releasing Energy
sections.body:
Cellular respiration breaks down glucose to produce ATP, the cell’s energy currency. It happens in three stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the citric acid cycle in the mitochondria, and oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport chain).

The net reaction is the reverse of photosynthesis: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + about 30‑32 ATP. Most of the ATP is made during oxidative phosphorylation.

Both plants and animals perform respiration, so the oxygen we breathe and the carbon dioxide we exhale are part of a global energy cycle.

sections.heading: Linking the Two Processes
sections.body:
Photosynthesis stores solar energy in glucose; respiration releases that energy for cellular work. The oxygen produced in photosynthesis is the same oxygen used in respiration, and the carbon dioxide released in respiration is the carbon source for photosynthesis.

This cycle connects all living organisms and drives ecosystems. When one group (plants) is affected, the whole energy flow can change.

key_terms.meaning: All chemical reactions that occur in a living cell.
Process by which plants convert light energy into chemical energy (glucose).
Breakdown of glucose to produce ATP, releasing CO₂ and H₂O.
Adenosine triphosphate, the main energy carrier in cells.
Organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place.
Organelle where most of cellular respiration occurs.

quiz.q: Which organelle is the site of photosynthesis?
quiz.why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and the machinery for photosynthesis.

quiz.q: What is the main product of glycolysis?
quiz.why: Glycolysis converts glucose into two molecules of pyruvate.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between photosynthesis and respiration?
options: Photosynthesis consumes glucose; respiration produces it.
Photosynthesis stores energy; respiration releases it.
They occur in the same organelle.
quiz.why: Photosynthesis stores solar energy in glucose, while respiration releases that stored energy as ATP.

quiz.q: How many ATP molecules are typically generated from one molecule of glucose during aerobic respiration?
quiz.why: Aerobic respiration yields about 30‑32 ATP per glucose molecule.

flashcards.front: What is the overall equation for photosynthesis?
Where does the electron transport chain occur in cellular respiration?
What molecule directly provides energy for most cellular activities?
Name the three stages of aerobic respiration.
flashcards.back: Glycolysis, citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle), oxidative phosphorylation.

flashcards.front: Why is oxygen essential for aerobic respiration?
flashcards.back: It acts as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain, allowing ATP production.
